turns.en: Man, the show notes on this episode are going to be out of control. It's going to hit some limit for [inaudible 00:53:20].
turns.zh: 天，这期的 show notes 要疯了。要撞上[听不清 00:53:20]的某个上限了。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yeah, maybe we're ... Yeah, the longest show notes ever. Sorry.
turns.zh: 对，也许我们……对，史上最长 show notes。抱歉。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God. Yeah, it's going to be rough. I'm actually going to try to get Nancy Duarte in this podcast.
turns.zh: 我的天。对，会很难搞。我其实想试着把 Nancy Duarte 弄进这播客。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Ooh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，好啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So that's a good ... That's-
turns.zh: 所以那是好……那是——

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Say hi if you do. Yeah, I'm a fan.
turns.zh: 如果你请到，替我问好。对，我是粉丝。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I'll do that. I'll do that. Okay. So getting to our final topic, which is around community. You're a big fan of finding community and just the power of being in a community, and I know you've done a bunch of research there, you're just like pumping your fist as we talk about this. I love it. So tell us why you're such a big fan of the power of community for product managers in general.
turns.zh: 好，我会那么做。我会那么做。好。那么我们来到最后一个话题——社群（community）。你是找社群、社群力量的大力粉丝，我知道你在那做了不少研究，我们聊这个时你就在那握拳。我爱了。所以跟我们说说，为什么你这么推崇社群对 PM 的力量。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Again, the starting point was a rather egocentric starting point because I'm constantly thinking about, how could I scale the work that I do because I still see so many companies not getting a product coach or I still see so many companies where people development is not a priority, all these kind of things. And at some point, I thought, if the line manager is not taking care of the personal development, who could? And I talked to several of my colleagues about the question and, at some point, somebody said, "Yeah, that's what community of practices are often used for." So that's where a lot of people get their inspiration. And basically, I reflected on my career. And early on, I was in a super engaging product organization where, really, we tried a lot, we shared a lot. A lot of the things that we tried didn't work at all, but others really fell on fertile grounds and we could learn from each other.
turns.zh: 再次，起点其实相当自我中心，因为我一直在想：我怎么把我做的工作规模化？因为我仍看到那么多公司不请产品教练，仍看到那么多公司不把人员发展当优先级，之类。有天我想：如果直线经理不照顾个人发展，谁能？我和几个同事聊了这个问题，有次有人说"对，那正是实践社群（community of practice）通常的用途。"所以那正是很多人获得启发的地方。然后我基本反思了我的职业。早年我在一个超投入的产品组织里，我们真试了很多、分享了很多。很多试的根本不行，但另一些真落在了沃土上，我们能互相学。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: And we invested quite some time in this sharing, but everyone got better over time because of this community being present. And so I decided to make this my topic for this year's research, so to say. And I was talking to a lot of my clients and former clients, "Hey, are you running a community of practice? If you don't run a community of practice, why is that?" Often, they have never considered running one, they don't know where to start. So that's another problem, obviously. And at some point, I decided to conduct a survey to see if random strangers can tell me about their companies and their community of practice. And it was super interesting as well.
turns.zh: 我们在这分享上投入了相当多时间，但每个人随时间都变好了，因为有这个社群在。所以我决定把这也做成我今年研究的主题。我和很多客户、前客户聊："嘿，你们在运营实践社群吗？如果没，为什么？"常是他们从没考虑过运营一个，不知道从哪开始。所以那显然是另一个问题。有天我决定做个调查，看随机陌生人能不能告诉我他们公司和他们的实践社群。也超有意思。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: For example, I found that oftentimes there is a bit of a community of practice internally, but they never heard about external product community. So they never heard of your community or to raise this community or mind the product or any of those external communities. And that is shocking to an extent as well because we're all so friendly human beings, happy to share what we learn, and they don't have to go through the same things over and over again. So that's why I think it's a super important question and I would love to help a bit more companies to start a community of practice or to mature the community of practice that they're already having.
turns.zh: 比如，我发现常常公司内部有点实践社群，但他们从没听说过外部产品社群。所以他们从没听说过你的社群、或 Raise The Bar 这个社群、或 Mind the Product、或任何那些外部社群。那在某种程度上也吓人，因为我们都是这么友好的人，乐意分享学到的，他们不必一遍遍经历同样的事。所以我觉得这是超重要的问题，我很想帮更多公司启动实践社群、或让他们已有的实践社群更成熟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What impact have you seen folks get when they join or find a great community? And then what are communities that you find are most useful? You mentioned ... And I want to get your advice on what I could do to make it even better, but maybe those two questions. What impact do you find when you find a great community and then what are some that you [inaudible 00:56:31]?
turns.zh: 你看到人们加入或找到好社群后获得什么影响？然后哪些社群你觉得最有用的？你提到了……我想就"我怎么让它更好"听你的建议，但也许先这两问。找到好社群时你发现什么影响，然后有哪些你[听不清 00:56:31]？

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: One impact, definitely, is stickiness. So people tend to stay with companies where they're learning and growing and can, yeah, get to mastery, so to say. Hello, Daniel Pink. So that is really something that people are thriving for, and if they find this in a company and a product community of practice could be a big part of that. So that is one impact.
turns.zh: 一个影响，绝对是"粘性"（stickiness）。人们倾向留在那些能学习、成长、能——怎么说——达到精通的公司。你好，Daniel Pink。那是人们真正渴望的，如果他们在公司里找到这个，而产品实践社群可以是其中很大一部分。所以那是一个影响。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Then the other impact, there's less people development on the desk of the product lead if there is a good product community of practice. So product leads, your life will get so much easier if there is a product community of practice. And it's actually a pretty cheap way of doing people development because trainings are expensive, conference tickets are expensive, getting external product coach, expensive. But helping people to learn from each other by making room for that and giving them a bit of time to reflect and to share what they're learning, that's rather cheap. So I think that is the benefits that I see.
turns.zh: 然后另一个影响：如果有好的产品实践社群，产品负责人桌上的人发展活就少了。所以产品负责人，如果有产品实践社群，你的生活会轻松太多。而且它其实是个相当便宜的人发展方式，因为培训贵、会议门票贵、外部产品教练贵。但帮人们互相学——腾出空间、给他们点时间反思和分享学到什么——那相当便宜。所以我觉得那是我看到的好处。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Training budget impact. People tend to stay with the company a bit longer. Leadership wise, it's less a time that you have to invest in people development. And then it's just fun for a lot of people. That's another uptake, I'd say.
turns.zh: 培训预算影响。人们倾向在公司多留一阵。领导力上，你投入人发展的时间少了。然后对很多人就是好玩。那是另一个好处，我觉得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are signs that the community that you're in, say, you found?You mentioned a bunch that I think are awesome. Teresa's community, we'll talk about my Slack a little bit. Mind the Product.
turns.zh: 你身处的社群、比如你找到了，有什么信号说明它是好社群、值得你花时间？是那种该留下，还是"算了，走人"？

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are signs that the community you're in is good with your time? Something you should stick with versus like, "Nah, get out of there."
turns.zh: 你身处的社群有什么信号说明它对得起你的时间？是该坚持，还是" nah，离开那"？

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: That is actually a good question. So I would say, if it helps you with networking, that is really something good if you meet nice, interesting people. So that is one thing I would love to mention. And then if you're learning something new every now and then, maybe not every day, maybe not every week, but every now and then, there should be some real nuggets where you think, "Oh, this is making my life easier," or "This is super interesting. I would never ever have stumbled upon this thing without the community." So learning something new and then reflecting on how much you already learned about a certain topic or know about a certain topic, which is contributing to the community.
turns.zh: 那其实是个好问题。我会说，如果它帮你建立人脉（networking），那真是个好东西——如果你遇到 nice、有趣的人。所以那是我想提的一点。然后如果你时不时能学到点新东西——也许不是每天、不是每周，但时不时——该有些真金子，让你想"哦，这让我的生活更容易了"或"这超有趣，没有这社群我绝不会撞上这个"。所以学到新东西，然后反思你在一个话题上已经学了多少、知道多少，那也是在对社群做贡献。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: You could be a community moderator, you could be somebody organizing some of the rituals, you could be somebody just sharing what you learned. So I think that is something that could be in a good community that is possible at least to share that everybody's sharing and that there's mutual trust and then it's often just, if you enjoy being part of this community. That's, I think, another super important thing to look into. Do you like the people there? Do you like to hang out with them? Do you think they're kind, lovely human beings? And is there some level of activity in the community because there's too many dead ones out there, more or less? And I think these are the things that I, yeah, would use as a benchmark.
turns.zh: 你可以当社群 moderator，可以当组织某些仪式的人，可以就当分享学到什么的人。所以我觉得那是一个好社群里可能有的——至少可能大家都在分享、有相互信任，而且通常就是：你是否享受作为社群一部分。那我觉得是另一个超重要、该看的点。你喜欢那里的人吗？你喜欢和他们混吗？你觉得他们善良、可爱吗？社群里有没有某种活跃度——因为外面死掉的社群太多了，多少算？我觉得这些是我会用作基准的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you're talking about this, initially, I was just imagining online communities, but there's also, obviously, offline communities probably somewhere in your local city.
turns.zh: 你聊这个时，一开始我只想到线上社群，但显然也有线下的、大概在你当地城市的。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yeah, product things.
turns.zh: 对，产品类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. Just like ... Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。就像……对。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So I think ... I don't know if people thought that when I was talking, but, yeah, there's probably meetups happening in your city with product managers that are meeting each other every week, every month maybe.
turns.zh: 对。所以我觉得……不知人们听我讲时是不是这么想，但，对，你城市里大概有 PM 聚会，每周、或也许每月互相见。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That sounds awesome. And I love your point about the why of the community versus a course versus reading lots of books. It's really affordable to join some product community, especially if it's online.
turns.zh: 那听起来超棒。我爱你说的——为什么是社群、而不是课程、而不是读很多书。加入某个产品社群真负担得起，尤其如果是在线的。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the ROI could be really high.
turns.zh: 而 ROI 可能真高。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yeah. And it brings so much clarity in your thinking if you're sharing some things you learned with the community that this is a massive uptake as well, so give back. That really makes sense for you personally as well.
turns.zh: 对。而且如果你和社群分享学到的东西，它会给你的思考带来超多清晰——那也是巨大的好处，所以要回馈。那对你个人也真有意义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you mentioned my Slack community. So if folks don't know this and they're listening, basically, if you're a paid subscriber committees letter, you get access to the Slack and there's about 10,000 people in there, mostly PMs and founders and growth leaders, and it's pretty damn incredible. It's probably the thing I'm most proud of of all the things I've done over the last few years around this newsletter and podcast.
turns.zh: 你提到了我的 Slack 社群。如果听的人不知道，基本就是：如果你是付费订阅我 newsletter 的，你就能进 Slack，里面大概一万人，大多是 PM、创始人和增长负责人，真的相当不可思议。那大概是我过去几年围绕 newsletter 和播客做的所有事里最骄傲的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so if you're not in there, you should definitely check it out. It's thriving. There's meetups happening all over the world every month. There's a mentorship program, there's mastermind groups, all kinds of stuff. And you're familiar with it. And so I just wanted to ask you while I have you here, do you have any advice for how to make this community even more great?
turns.zh: 所以如果你不在里面，你绝对该去看看。它很兴旺。全世界每月都有聚会。有导师项目、有 mastermind 小组、各种东西。你也熟悉它。所以我只是趁你在，想问你：对我怎么让这个社群更棒，有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: That is not an easy question. First of all, congratulations. I really think it's a massive achievement to start such a community and to really have such a vibrant community because I know it takes a lot of energy investment at first to get it going and then a lot of energy to keep it on a certain level, so to say.
turns.zh: 那不是个容易的问题。首先，恭喜。我真觉得启动这样一个社群、并真有个这么有活力的社群，是巨大的成就，因为我知道一开始要让它动起来要投入大量精力，然后要保持在一定水平也要大量精力。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yeah. What I found helpful is I have this community canvas that I use when I'm working with clients and some of these things require workshops to some extent. So it helps to reflect on what is the purpose of the community and that changes over time with the community members that are currently part of this community, right? So that is not a stable thing. So sometimes everybody has to pause for a second and then think about what is the purpose of this community, what are our values, and how will we define success?
turns.zh: 对。我发现有用的是：我有个"社群画布"（community canvas），我和客户工作时用，其中一些事在某种程度上需要工作坊。所以它帮人反思：社群的目的是什么——而那随当前社群成员变化，对吧？所以不是稳定的事。所以有时大家都得停一下，想想社群的目的是什么、我们的价值观是什么、我们怎么定义成功？

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: It's pretty boring, I know, because it sounds so, so familiar with what we do in product management, but I think it applies for product communities as well. And then you need to find good rituals and rhythm, and you, Lenny, were already talking about some of the ones you are using. I know, for example, what Teresa is doing in her community. I interviewed her this year, so there is a blog post on that online as well where she talks about what she tried, and what did work, and what did not work. So I think that is important.
turns.zh: 我知道那挺无聊，因为听起来和我们产品管理做的太熟了，但我觉得它也适用于产品社群。然后你需要找到好的仪式和节奏，而你 Lenny 已经聊了你在用的一些。比如我知道 Teresa 在她社群里做什么。我今年采访了她，所以网上也有篇关于那的博客，她讲她试了什么、什么管用、什么不管用。所以我觉得那重要。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Then maybe not so important for your community. Well, let's see. Let's discuss, let me hear what you think, which is incentives and sponsoring. So how do you, yeah, value contribution? Are you giving back? Is it a kudos mechanism or is it something where people really earn badges of honor or earn time, earn more training budget. That's what a lot of companies do, right? If you're playing an active role in the community, then you get more training budget to spend or something like that, or they grant you time to do so. So if you say like, "Hey, I want to be part of this product community, could I travel a quarter or something like that because I want to go and see those people?" That is something that people do. So incentives and sponsoring, then it's roles. And that will be interesting in your case as well. Is Lenny the center of the community?
turns.zh: 然后也许对你的社群没那么重要。嗯，看看。我们讨论下，听你怎么想——是激励和赞助。你怎么，对，重视贡献？你在回馈吗？是那种 kudos（点赞致谢）机制，还是人们真赚荣誉徽章、或赚时间、赚更多培训预算？很多公司就这么做，对吧？如果你在社群里活跃，就给你更多培训预算花，或之类，或他们给你时间去做。比如你说"嘿，我想参与这个产品社群，我能每季度出差一下吗，因为我想去见那些人？"人们就那么做。所以激励和赞助，然后是角色。你这 case 也挺有趣。Lenny 是社群的中心吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I try really hard not to do that, actually.
turns.zh: 对，其实我真的努力不那样做。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yeah, right. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对，正是。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a [inaudible 01:03:36] try to not be the beacon of all answers. The actual goal of the community was I will not have all the answers. Let's just bring a bunch of smart people together that are already there's this interesting filter of who pays for content about product and growth and stuff.
turns.zh: 那是[听不清 01:03:36]努力不做所有答案的灯塔。社群真正的目标是：我不会拥有所有答案。就把一群聪明人聚一起——而这里有个有趣的过滤器：谁会为关于产品和增长的内容付费。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Filter's really interesting. So the whole idea was get out of the middle of this thing and let people help each other and it's worked out really well.
turns.zh: 过滤器真有意思。所以整个想法是：从中间退出来，让人们互相帮助——而它运作得真不错。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yeah, because that's what I would say after doing all this research, it's not sustainable if the whole community is on the shoulders of one, two, three people. So you need to distribute the workload and you need to distribute this responsibility because sometimes even things like, yeah, policing the community is not a pleasant job. And if there's only one person dealing with all of these things, then it's not really community because then it's a bit organized like a company in this pyramid scheme.
turns.zh: 对，因为那是我做了所有研究后会说的：如果整个社群压在一、二、三个人肩上，是不可持续的。所以你得把工作量分散、把责任分散，因为有时甚至像"治理社群"都不是愉快的工作。如果只有一个人处理所有这些，那它就不是真社群，因为那有点像公司式的金字塔结构。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: So I think more of it as circles, different circles of interest, and then building bridges between them because maybe not everybody in your community is interested in the same topics, but maybe they are the smaller circles of 10, 15 people interested in this one topic, 10, 15 people interested in this other topic. You may be connecting the dots, you may be giving a bit of impulse and inspiration, but maybe other people are doing the exact same thing, sharing their best reads and their worthy to watch videos, and all these kind of things. So content and curation, definitely, is another thing that you should think about and reflect on once in a while.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得更多把它想成圆圈、不同的兴趣圈，然后在它们之间架桥——因为也许不是你社群里每个人都对同一话题感兴趣，但也许有 10、15 人的小圈对这一个话题感兴趣，10、15 人对另一个话题感兴趣。你也许在连点，也许给点推动和启发，但也许别人在做完全一样的事、分享他们最好的读物、值得看的视频，之类。所以内容和策展（curation）绝对是另一件你该时不时想、反思的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Thanks for the advice. Curious is so important. Especially early on, I found keeping the signal to noise high always. And especially early on, it was a really prayerful. So there's a lot of focus [inaudible 01:05:19] detail oriented about it all.
turns.zh: 酷。谢谢建议。好奇心真重要。尤其早期，我发现一直保持高信噪比。尤其早期，那是真的很用心。所以有很多聚焦[听不清 01:05:19]对细节的在意。

turns.speaker: Petra Wille
turns.en: Yeah. Plus, a lot of communities that I see use engagement as a success metric, and I'm actually not sure if this is a good success metric. So as you say, signal versus noise is maybe the better success metric, which leads us the down the rabbit hole of how to [inaudible 01:05:38]. But, yeah, engagement is maybe not the predominant success factor for a community.
turns.zh: 对。加上，我看到的很多社群把参与度（engagement）当成功指标，而我其实不确定这是不是好指标。所以如你所说，信噪比也许是更好的成功指标——那把我们带进"怎么[听不清 01:05:38]"的兔子洞。但，对，参与度也许不是社群主导的成功因素。
